title: Sony Music moves to add more than 30,000 copyrighted recordings to its lawsuit against Udio

reading.body:
An AI music generation system was deployed and made available to millions of users while its training data remained legally contested. The core failure here is a system built on copyrighted material without prior authorization from rights holders, a practice that only became visible as a legal problem after deployment was already underway. The point in the pipeline where this could have been caught was at the data-curation stage, before training, by clearing rights or using only licensed recordings.

The incident produced several distinct legal threads simultaneously: one major label settled and moved toward a licensing partnership, another filed a new lawsuit alleging its recordings were used without permission, and independent artists pursued a separate class action. A court declined to dismiss the independent artists' case and allowed it to proceed in a different jurisdiction. These are active legal proceedings, not findings, and no court has yet ruled on whether Udio's training constituted infringement.

What the incident shows about deployment practice is that the commercial launch preceded any licensing framework, and the eventual settlement required building that framework retroactively. The announced future platform, trained on authorized music, implicitly acknowledges that the original system was not.

summary:
Universal Music Group has settled a lawsuit against AI music startup Udio, which was accused of using copyrighted songs to train its artificial intelligence system. The case involved allegations that Udio generated music similar to existing hits, including The Temptations' "My Girl." Under the new licensing agreements, Udio will launch a platform next year trained exclusively on authorized and licensed music, allowing users to create, customize, and share songs while compensating artists and songwriters involved.

This settlement represents Udio's first major licensing deal with a major music label and signals a shift toward cooperation between AI companies and the entertainment industry. Udio's CEO stated the partnership would unite AI and the music industry while supporting artists. The startup, launched in 2024 by former Google DeepMind employees and backed by investors including will.i.am, has attracted millions of users since its release. UMG did not disclose financial terms of the agreement and simultaneously announced a separate partnership with Stability AI to develop music creation tools for artists and producers.
